title: Episode 159: Theodore Roosevelt and the Bull Moose Campaign: The Bullet and the 90-Minute Speech (1912)
description:
In 1912, Theodore Roosevelt staged the most dramatic third-party insurgency in American history. Disillusioned by the conservative turn of his handpicked successor William Howard Taft, TR broke with the Republican Party and launched the Progressive 'Bull Moose' crusade, declaring: 'We stand at Armageddon, and we battle for the Lord!' Then, on October 14, 1912, outside the Gilpatrick Hotel in Milwaukee, a deranged saloonkeeper shot Roosevelt in the chest at point-blank range. With blood soaking through his shirt and a bullet lodged an inch from his heart, Roosevelt refused hospital care, walked onto the stage of the Milwaukee Auditorium, and delivered a legendary ninety-minute speech: 'It takes more than that to kill a Bull Moose!' Discover the greatest display of physical courage in presidential history.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our portrait of Theodore Roosevelt with an epic saga of political rebellion and superhuman physical courage. In 1912, Roosevelt challenged the very party he had once led, championing a revolutionary vision of social justice, women's suffrage, and healthcare—and proved that not even an assassin's bullet could silence his voice. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: REGRET IN THE RED ROOM
On the evening of November 8, 1904, having just won the presidency in a historic popular landslide, forty-six-year-old Theodore Roosevelt walked into the Red Room of the White House and issued a statement that he would regret for the rest of his life. Surrendering to a wave of impulsive modesty, Roosevelt announced to reporters: 'The wise custom which limits the President to two terms regards the substance and not the form, and under no circumstances will I be a candidate for or accept another nomination.' His wife Edith, standing nearby, whispered to a friend: 'Theodore has just made a terrible mistake.'\n\nRoosevelt was at the absolute summit of his popularity and vigor, but he had tied his own hands. When his term ended in March 1909, Roosevelt handpicked his closest friend and loyal Secretary of War, William Howard Taft, to succeed him, believing Taft would carry forward the torch of progressive reform. To give Taft room to govern without interference, Roosevelt immediately fled the country, embarking on a grueling year-long safari through British East Africa, where he shot over five hundred big game specimens for the Smithsonian Institution, followed by a triumphal tour of European monarchies.\n\nRoosevelt's pledge to step down in 1908 had been made in the euphoria of victory, but as the years passed, his boundless physical energy and reforming zeal made quiet retirement impossible. He felt like an exiled warrior watching his hard-won victories being compromised by lesser men.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE BITTER DISILLUSIONMENT
When Roosevelt returned to New York in June 1910, greeted by five million cheering citizens who lined the harbor, he found the Republican Party in civil war. Progressive Republicans, led by Senator Robert M. La Follette of Wisconsin and Gifford Pinchot, accused President Taft of surrendering to conservative party bosses, signing the protective Payne-Aldrich Tariff, and firing Pinchot from the Forest Service over western coal lands.\n\nRoosevelt tried to remain neutral, but Taft's legalistic, cautious approach infuriated him. In August 1910, Roosevelt delivered his famous 'New Nationalism' speech in Osawatomie, Kansas, advocating a sweeping progressive platform: women's suffrage, a federal income tax, an eight-hour workday, an end to child labor, workman's compensation, and national health insurance. When Taft's Justice Department filed an antitrust suit against United States Steel, specifically citing a merger Roosevelt had personally approved in 1907, TR felt personally betrayed and insulted. In February 1912, Roosevelt made his fateful announcement: 'My hat is in the ring. The fight is on and I am stripped to the buff!'\n\nThe New Nationalism speech in Kansas outlined a revolutionary charter for modern American liberalism, arguing that human rights and social welfare must take precedence over corporate property rights. Roosevelt declared that the state must intervene directly to ensure economic fairness for every citizen.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE THEFT AT THE CHICAGO COLISEUM
The 1912 Republican primary campaign was a ferocious, personal brawl between two former best friends. For the first time in American history, thirteen states held direct presidential primaries. Roosevelt won nine of them, including Taft's home state of Ohio, capturing over seventy percent of all primary votes cast. The Republican rank-and-file overwhelmingly wanted Roosevelt.\n\nHowever, the conservative party machine, led by Senator Boies Penrose and William Barnes, controlled the Republican National Committee. At the convention in Chicago in June 1912, the bosses fraudulently awarded over two hundred contested delegate seats to Taft, locking Roosevelt out of the nomination. Infuriated by the blatant corruption, Roosevelt commanded his delegates to boycott the proceedings. Walking over to the nearby Orchestra Hall, Roosevelt addressed a wild, roaring crowd of thousands: 'We stand at Armageddon, and we battle for the Lord!' The Progressive Party—the 'Bull Moose Party'—was born.\n\nThe conservative party bosses were willing to suffer catastrophic electoral defeat rather than allow Roosevelt to regain control of the Republican Party and dismantle their patronage apparatus. They used procedural technicalities to deny seats to delegates who had been elected by overwhelming primary majorities.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE PROGRESSIVE CRUSADE AND THE BULL MOOSE
The Progressive National Convention in August 1912 was unlike any political gathering in American history. It had the evangelical fervor of a religious revival, with delegates singing hymns like 'Onward, Christian Soldiers' and 'The Battle Hymn of the Republic.' Jane Addams, the founder of Hull House and the foremost social reformer in America, seconded Roosevelt's nomination. The Progressive platform was decades ahead of its time, pioneering the foundations of the modern American welfare state: universal social security, unemployment insurance, a living wage, direct election of senators, and the vote for women.\n\nAsked by reporters if he felt physically fit to undertake a grueling three-way race against Taft and the brilliant Democratic nominee Woodrow Wilson, Roosevelt grinned ferociously and replied: 'I am as strong as a bull moose!' The moniker caught fire with the press. Roosevelt barnstormed the country by train, drawing colossal crowds in major cities and challenging the entrenched powers of Wall Street and machine politics.\n\nThe Progressive Party convention drew idealistic social workers, suffragists, university professors, and trade unionists, united by an evangelical zeal to cleanse American public life of corporate corruption. The singing of gospel hymns gave the movement the intensity of a moral crusade.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SHOT OUTSIDE THE GILPATRICK HOTEL
On the evening of Monday, October 14, 1912, Roosevelt was in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, preparing to deliver a major address at the Milwaukee Auditorium. After eating a light dinner at the Gilpatrick Hotel, Roosevelt walked out the front doors at eight o'clock and stepped into an open touring car. A crowd of hundreds cheered as Roosevelt stood up in the car, lifted his hat, and smiled.\n\nSuddenly, out of the shadows, a thirty-six-year-old Bavarian immigrant and former saloonkeeper named John Flammang Schrank pushed forward. Schrank was a delusional madman who claimed that the ghost of William McKinley had appeared to him in a dream, pointing at Roosevelt and saying: 'This is my murderer! Avenge my death!' Standing barely five feet away, Schrank leveled a .38-caliber Colt revolver directly at Roosevelt's chest and pulled the trigger. A blinding flash and a deafening gunshot shattered the evening air. The force of the bullet knocked Roosevelt backward onto the leather seat. Roosevelt's stenographer, a former football player named Elbert Martin, instantly tackled Schrank to the pavement, pinning him down while furious spectators shouted: 'Lynch him! Kill him!'\n\nSchrank had stalked Roosevelt across eight southern and midwestern states for weeks, waiting for a clear moment in an open automobile to execute his delusional mission. He believed that killing Roosevelt would enforce the unwritten two-term tradition and avenge McKinley's memory.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE MIRACULOUS SHIELD
Roosevelt stood up in the car, waved his hand to calm the screaming crowd, and shouted: 'Don't hurt him! Bring him here! I want to look at him.' Schrank was hauled to the car; Roosevelt looked into the assassin's wild eyes, asked: 'Why did you do it?', and when Schrank remained silent, turned him over to the police. Roosevelt reached inside his coat. His fingers came away covered in warm, sticky blood. He coughed softly into his hand; seeing no blood in his saliva, Roosevelt's anatomical knowledge told him that the bullet had not pierced his lung.\n\nWhat had saved Theodore Roosevelt's life was an astonishing stroke of luck. In the breast pocket of his heavy wool coat, Roosevelt was carrying two items: a dense, fifty-page handwritten speech folded in half, and an all-metal spectacle case. The heavy lead bullet had smashed through the steel case, tore through all one hundred layers of folded paper, penetrated his wool coat, flannel shirt, and undershirt, fractured his fourth rib, and came to rest embedded three inches deep in the muscle of his chest wall, barely one inch from his heart. Had the speech and spectacle case not slowed the bullet's velocity, it would have entered his heart and killed him instantly.\n\nThe fifty-page manuscript, filled with Roosevelt's dense revisions and rhetorical flourishes, absorbed the kinetic energy of the heavy lead bullet, turning a fatal assassination into a survivable wound. The steel spectacle case shattered under the impact, deflecting the bullet away from his ribs.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: 'IT TAKES MORE THAN THAT TO KILL A BULL MOOSE'
Doctors rushed forward, urging Roosevelt to go immediately to the hospital. Roosevelt flatly refused: 'I will deliver this speech or die,' he told them. 'It is more important than my life.' Roosevelt arrived at the Milwaukee Auditorium, where nine thousand spectators were waiting. Walking to the podium, pale and shivering from shock, Roosevelt held up his bloody, perforated manuscript and spoke in a hoarse, quiet voice that silenced the cavernous hall:\n\n'Friends, I shall ask you to be as quiet as possible. I do not know whether you fully understand that I have just been shot; but it takes more than that to kill a Bull Moose!' The audience gasped in horror as Roosevelt opened his coat, revealing his white shirt soaked in dark red blood. Despite the pleas of his aides, Roosevelt spoke for ninety minutes, passionately explaining his vision of social justice, before walking off the stage under his own power to be taken to Emergency Hospital.\n\nIn November, Roosevelt achieved the greatest third-party result in American history, winning 4.1 million votes and eighty-eight electoral votes, completely humiliating William Howard Taft, who carried only eight electoral votes. While the Republican split handed the presidency to Democrat Woodrow Wilson, Theodore Roosevelt had established an immortal legend of physical heroism. He was the living embodiment of the strenuous life, proving that the spirit of an authentic leader is unconquerable.\n\nRoosevelt's refusal to leave the stage until his speech was finished became an enduring legend of American stoicism, proving that physical courage was the ultimate foundation of his political creed. He held the audience spellbound for an hour and a half while blood dripped down his side.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Theodore Roosevelt's Bull Moose campaign redefined the boundaries of progressive reform and provided the supreme demonstration of executive physical bravery in American annals. His vision of social democracy would later be realized by his cousin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Next week, we turn our attention to the man TR defeated for second place—William Howard Taft—the genial Ohio jurist whose heart belonged to the law, and who achieved his ultimate life's dream not in the White House, but as Chief Justice of the United States. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
